sizeReason: The team has 52 hours across three people, so medium fits despite the 24-hour deadline. Keep every section short and focus on a reliable demo. Without live university data, show student-reported activity and unknown status, not guaranteed availability.

parts.summary: Build a phone-friendly room finder for campus students, with a clear live demonstration for the judges. Show room names, buildings and recent student check-ins.
parts.details:
The app cannot know which rooms are actually free: the university PDF supplies locations, not bookings or occupancy. Show “No recent reports” or “3 active check-ins,” with a clear explanation that reports do not guarantee availability. Students can check in and check out. Old check-ins expire so forgotten departures do not remain forever.

Noor owns design, room-list checking and the pitch. Tom owns the React interface. Ilias owns the Flask service and shared check-in records. Build everything during the hackathon, use no paid services and include no AI.

Success at hour 24: judges see two phones open the same room list, one check in, the other refresh to see the count change, then check out.

parts.summary: Ship a room list, shared check-in counts, check-in, check-out and a rehearsed three-minute demo. Plan 36 person-hours and reserve 16 of the available 52 hours for delays and fixes.
parts.details:
Start with a small, verified selection of rooms from the PDF. Include building names, empty and error states, automatic expiry, and a refresh control. Defer the map, notifications, university login and noise reports: none is needed to demonstrate the main benefit.

Hours 0–2: agree labels, room data and the messages exchanged by the interface and service. Noor designs; Tom and Ilias build their separate areas using the agreed examples.

By hour 12: show a phone-sized list, check in, refresh a second browser and check out using shared records.

Hours 12–18: finish expiry, errors and connection setup. Freeze features at hour 18. Hours 18–22: test phones and fix failures. Hours 22–24: rehearse and prepare the demo.

Planned loads: Noor 11/16 hours; Tom 12.5/18; Ilias 12.5/18. The remaining 16 hours are contingency, not extra features.

parts.summary: Use React and Flask in one repository and one deployed web service. Store check-ins in PostgreSQL. This fits Tom’s and Ilias’s existing skills and the free budget.
parts.details: Tom knows React; Ilias knows Flask. PostgreSQL stores records across server restarts; their experience with it is unknown. Budget 2 person-hours for deployment, 1 for database learning within backend work, and 1.5 for local fallback setup and verification. Use the same PostgreSQL implementation locally and online. Flask serves the built React page and data routes. Render’s free database has 1 GB storage, expires after 30 days, and lacks managed backups. Its free web service sleeps after 15 idle minutes and takes about a minute to wake. [Free-plan limits](https://render.com/docs/free). Prove hosted reads and writes by hour 4. Build all code, assets, and demo material during the event.

parts.summary: Show a room list grouped by building. Display active check-ins and when the page last refreshed. Counts cannot prove that a room is free or full.
parts.details: React requests counts every 15 seconds while visible and immediately after a write. Flask validates requests and commits each change as one transaction: all changes succeed together or none does. One browser has one active check-in; switching rooms replaces it. Repeated requests must not add extra check-ins. Expire reports after 60 minutes, with explicit renewal. Pure functions handle expiry and labels, with server time passed as input. Thin outer layers handle network calls, storage, and the clock. Keep files below about 400 lines and reuse rules. Show connection failures and stale data. Target the shared two-phone flow at hour 12 and freeze features at hour 18. Cut optional polish if either checkpoint slips. Protect hours 18–24 for testing, blocking fixes, and rehearsal.

decisions.why: Tap a room, then tap “I’m here.” Show confirmation only after the server accepts it. Keep a “Your check-in” link visible for quick checkout. Include explicit renewal and expiry in this same layout.

risks.risk: Students read zero check-ins as proof that a room is free.
risks.action: Use “availability unknown,” explain reports near the count, and test whether a peer understands this.

risks.risk: Old or failed updates appear current.
risks.action: Show update time and a stale-data message. Preserve the last known count with a warning; never replace failures with zero.

risks.risk: Phone-sized text is unreadable during the pitch.
risks.action: Test the projected view, enlarge the browser and rehearse one short path with clearly labelled demo activity.

tasks.title: Noor: sketch three screens and agree honest status wording; include in the manager’s design estimate
Noor: define shared controls and empty, loading, failure, renewal and expired states; include in design
Tom: implement phone layouts, styling, keyboard focus and renewal/expiry controls; include in frontend
Tom: check phone and keyboard flows, including renewal and expiry; fix clarity issues; include in testing
Noor: prepare and rehearse the three-minute pitch; include in presentation

checklist.answer: Students use phones to find rooms. Judges view the same flow on a projected browser during the three-minute pitch.
Room list finds rooms by building. Room detail explains activity and offers check-in. Your check-in shows expiry, renewal and checkout, or a return to check-in after expiry.
Open list → tap room → “I’m here.” Open Your check-in to check out or explicitly renew for 60 minutes from renewal. After expiry, tap “I’m here” again.

List: “No rooms listed,” loading, or retry. Detail: zero means unknown availability; loading disables actions; failure offers retry. Your check-in: no visit links to rooms; expired offers “I’m here”; saving disables repeat taps; failure offers retry without claiming success.
Use at least 16px body text, strong text contrast, large tap areas and words alongside colours. Check all actions with a keyboard and visible focus; announce save results to screen readers.
Plain labels, spacious cards, a restrained bright accent and immediate action feedback make the app friendly and fast.
All screens share the header, room information and status styles. Detail and Your check-in share one layout, including renewal and expired states, within Tom’s existing 6 hours.
Free/busy labels overstate what voluntary reports prove. Show reported activity and unknown availability. Prefer the permitted list option because the PDF provides no map locations.

challenges.idea: Show which rooms are free right now and filling up.
challenges.problem: No check-ins does not mean empty. Check-in counts do not reveal remaining seats, bookings or people who never checked in.
challenges.better: Show reported check-in counts with update times and explicit uncertainty. Present this as a student reporting tool, with demo activity clearly labelled.

questions: Which rows of the manager’s 36-hour estimate include these 12 hours? Proposed mapping: Noor 4 hours design and 2 presentation; Tom 4 frontend and 2 testing. This leaves at most Noor 10, Tom 12 and Ilias 18 hours for other work; confirm the remaining 24 planned hours fit those limits without double counting.
What display and internet connection will be available for the live pitch?

problems.problem: The two-phone milestone moves from hour 12 to hour 16, and the feature freeze moves from hour 18 to hour 20. This cuts the agreed testing and rehearsal window.
problems.fix: Target the shared two-phone flow at hour 12 and freeze features at hour 18. Cut optional work if those checkpoints slip.

problems.problem: Architecture tasks have no named owners, and their hours are not mapped into the manager’s 36-hour plan. Deployment alone rises from 2 to 3 hours, with a second database implementation also proposed.
problems.fix: Assign each task to Noor, Tom or Ilias and map it to the existing task budget. Include database learning and fallback work explicitly; keep planned work within 36 hours and each person’s allocation.

problems.problem: The seven security hours are not identified as replacements, included work or extra work. Tasks lack named owners, and one combines the React interface with the pitch.
problems.fix: Map security work into the manager’s existing tasks, assign one owner per task, and split interface work from pitch wording. Recalculate totals without spending the 30% buffer on planned work.

problems.problem: The twelve design, interface and rehearsal hours have no task owners or mapping to the manager’s estimates. The claim that they fit individual limits cannot yet be checked.
problems.fix: Assign design and presentation tasks to Noor and interface tasks to Tom. Mark which existing estimates include this work and reconcile the totals with the 36-hour plan.

problems.problem: Deleting expired records within five minutes cannot be guaranteed by the proposed cleanup during requests. The hosted service can sleep, and no requests may arrive.
problems.fix: For this prototype, exclude expired entries from counts immediately, delete them on the next request, and have Ilias clear stored records after the event. State this actual retention behavior instead of promising five-minute deletion.

problems.problem: The plan promises protected cookies and HTTPS, but the laptop fallback does not explain how phones will connect securely. Secure cookies will not work over ordinary HTTP to a laptop’s network address.
problems.fix: Define the fallback as two browsers on the presenting laptop using an explicit local-only configuration, or budget and test HTTPS access for phones. Keep any relaxed cookie settings restricted to local development.

problems.problem: The proposed label “3 students checked in” implies three distinct people, although the identity decision explicitly permits one person to report through several browsers.
problems.fix: Use “3 active check-ins” consistently in responses, screens and pitch examples.

problems.problem: The design leaves expiry as an unanswered question, although architecture and security specify 60 minutes and explicit renewal. The screens provide no renewal or expired-check-in flow.
problems.fix: Include expiry time and a renewal control in the existing check-in screen. Define its expired state and the return to check-in, within the current interface budget.

problems.problem: Cookie-based write authorization is specified, but protection against another website causing unwanted check-ins or checkouts is absent from the architecture.
problems.fix: Have Ilias add explicit SameSite cookie settings and server checks of request origin for writes. Include a test that rejects a write originating from another site.

choices.question: The manager’s detailed allocation was not supplied. How should the 24 architecture hours be reconciled with the existing 36-hour plan?
options: Map these tasks into the manager’s existing buckets, retaining the 2-hour deployment cap and named owners.
Adopt the provisional 36-hour envelope of Noor 10, Tom 12, and Ilias 14, then map the remaining panel work into it.

merge.title: Campus Room Reports

summaries.summary: Help students find rooms using recent student reports. Show active check-in counts and “Availability unknown”: the PDF cannot prove rooms are free, busy or full.

Build a building-grouped list, check-in, checkout, renewal and automatic expiry for a small verified room selection. Defer maps, notifications, university login and noise reports. Create all project work during the event; use free tools and no AI.

Tom builds the interface in React; Ilias builds the service in Flask, serving both from one address. Use PostgreSQL for shared records, subject to an early setup check. Cap online deployment work at 2 person-hours; keep a laptop demonstration available.

Noor owns design, room content and presentation; Tom owns the interface and integration checks; Ilias owns rules, storage and operation. Keep rules in small pure functions, with storage, network and clock access outside them. Keep files around 400 lines or less and reuse shared rules.

Store verified room names and buildings, plus each anonymous browser’s current room and expiry. Allow one active check-in per browser; switching replaces it, and reports expire after 60 minutes unless explicitly renewed. Publish counts only; delete expired records on requests and clear remaining records after the event.

Use protected browser cookies, encrypted web traffic, server-side ownership checks and limits on repeated requests. Reject changes from other websites; keep secrets and identifying tokens out of logs. Collect no names, location tracking or visit history; anonymous reports cannot verify physical presence.

Noor designs a friendly phone list, room detail and current check-in view using shared layouts. Use readable text, large controls, visible keyboard focus and words alongside colours. Show update time, renewal and expiry; failed updates must never appear as zero reports.

The supplied manager breakdown supports 36 planned person-hours: Noor 11/16, Tom 12.5/18 and Ilias 12.5/18, leaving 16 hours of buffer (30.8%). Expert estimates overlap these tasks; they are not additional hours. Show shared reports at hour 12, freeze features at hour 18, and protect the final block for rehearsal and fixes.

Main threats are misleading availability claims, setup delays, false reports and demo connectivity. Questions remain about PDF permission, event rules, hosting access, database experience, campus rules and presentation equipment. Resolve these early; use a clearly labelled local demonstration if public operation cannot be established.

tasks.title: Hours 0-4: Agree request examples, ownership, activity labels and expiry rules with Tom and Noor; document the shared contract (1 hour)
Hours 0-4: Sketch three phone views and agree honest status wording; check event rules on libraries and supplied materials (2 hours)
Hours 0-4: Set up React and build against the agreed example messages (2 hours)
Hours 0-4: Set up the repository and prove one hosted PostgreSQL read and write; check free allowances, encrypted access and secret settings; stop at the deployment cap (2 hours)
Hours 4-8: Verify permission and transcribe a small PDF room selection; label its limited coverage (2 hours)
Hours 4-8: Define shared controls and loading, empty, failure, renewal and expired states (2 hours)
Hours 4-8: Build the phone list and reusable room detail layout with readable styling and keyboard focus (3 hours)
Hours 4-8: Learn PostgreSQL within a 1-hour cap; implement pure validation, expiry and repeat-safe rules with focused tests using supplied time values (4 hours total)
Hours 8-12: Add protected browser identity, room totals, ownership checks, safe room switching, renewal, checkout, request limits and expired-record cleanup (4 hours)
Hours 8-12: Add check-in, checkout, renewal, privacy text, expiry and refresh controls; connect completed service routes and show the shared two-browser flow by hour 12 (3 hours)
Hours 8-12: Draft the three-minute pitch around student impact, honest limitations and the live demonstration (2 hours)

Hours 12-18: Finish 15-second visible-page updates, slower retries after failures and stale-data messages; verify two sessions, repeated writes, ownership, rejected cross-site changes and saved records (2.5 hours)
Hours 12-18: Test invalid inputs, ownership, forged requests, simultaneous duplicate writes and expiry; fix service failures (1 hour, following rule tests in T8)
Hours 12-18: Document startup and rehearse local PostgreSQL with two separate laptop browser profiles; bind the fallback to the laptop only (1.25 hours)
Hours 18-22: Test phone and keyboard flows, renewal, expiry and connection failures; fix blocking interface and clarity problems (2 hours)
Hours 18-22: Check projected readability and record a working backup demo, clearly labelled as recorded activity (1 hour)
Hours 22-24: Rehearse the timed pitch and both demo paths, prepare the presentation and deliver at hour 24; use buffer only for blocking fixes (2 hours)
Hours 22-24: Keep the cleanup checklist ready; immediately after the pitch clear check-ins and sessions and stop public operation (0.25 hour reserved for post-event cleanup)

merge.halfwayDemo: At hour 12, show a phone-sized room list, check in from one browser, refresh another to see the shared count, then check out; use two phones if hosting works.

risks.risk: Reports are mistaken for verified availability or reservations.
risks.action: Use “active check-ins” and “availability unknown” throughout. Explain that counts do not establish remaining seats or reserve rooms; have a peer explain the labels back to Noor.

risks.risk: The open allocation discussion causes expert estimates to be added twice.
risks.action: The detailed manager breakdown is present in this brief, so use its 36-hour total as the working baseline. Open options: mapping expert work into these buckets preserves named owners and the 2-hour deployment cap, but requires combining overlapping work; adopting Noor 10, Tom 12 and Ilias 14 shifts effort toward the service, but leaves Ilias less than a 30% personal buffer and requires a new mapping. Do not schedule that alternative as extra work.

risks.risk: Database setup and security work exceed Ilias’s 12.5 planned hours.
risks.action: Ask about PostgreSQL experience and laptop support at the start. All security and architecture work is included, not additive. Stop online setup after 2 hours; protect ownership and expiry checks, cut polish, and use the reserved buffer only for necessary fixes.

risks.risk: Hosting or venue connectivity prevents the live demonstration.
risks.action: Confirm a free hosting account, current allowances, venue internet and display access. Online hosting supports two phones but brings setup and connection risk; laptop operation avoids venue internet but demonstrates two browser profiles instead. Verify the chosen path early, rehearse the laptop fallback and retain Noor’s labelled recording.

risks.risk: The interface and service do not work together by hour 12.
risks.action: Agree example messages in T1 and connect routes as Ilias completes them during hours 8-12. At hour 12 require the shared check-in and checkout flow. Freeze features at hour 18 and drop visual polish if the checkpoint slips.

risks.risk: False, repeated or forgotten reports distort counts.
risks.action: Allow one active room per browser, make retries safe, switch rooms in one database transaction and expire reports after 60 minutes. Limit repeated writes and explain that several browsers can still represent one person.

risks.risk: Forged requests or exposed records reveal or alter attendance.
risks.action: Use hashed random tokens in storage and protected cookies. Require an exact matching website origin for changes, derive ownership on the server and disable public debug output. Test two independent sessions, avoid token logs and clear records after the pitch; allow relaxed encryption settings only in explicit laptop-only mode.

risks.risk: Unconfirmed event or campus rules prevent the planned use.
risks.action: Questions: Are standard libraries and the supplied PDF allowed? May room names be republished? Which country and campus rules apply to presence reports? Is the entry intended for public use or judges only? Resolve before publication; use clearly labelled fictional rooms and a local demonstration if permission remains unknown.

risks.risk: Old data looks current or the demo is unreadable.
risks.action: Show the last successful update and a warning after failures; never substitute zero. Test phone text, keyboard controls and the presentation display. Confirm server acceptance before showing a successful check-in.

glossary.meaning: One hour of work by one person; several people can work during the same elapsed hour.
Time reserved for delays and necessary fixes rather than planned features.
A JavaScript library Tom can use to build the browser interface.
A Python framework Ilias can use to serve the app and handle requests.
A database that stores shared room and check-in records.
Setting up the application so it runs on its demonstration or public server.
The shared project folder with a recorded history of file changes.
A function that calculates a result from supplied inputs without reading or changing outside systems.
The agreed format and meaning of messages between the interface and service.
A service address that handles a particular request, such as checking out.
A check that separately built parts work correctly together.
A small value the browser stores and sends back to the app to identify its session.
A temporary browser identity that lets the service recognise and protect that browser’s check-in.
A one-way representation of a random secret, stored instead of the secret itself.
The website address a browser request comes from, checked before accepting a change.
A protected connection that prevents others on the network from reading the app’s messages.
A group of database changes that all succeed together or leave the records unchanged.
Repeating the same request does not create additional check-ins.
A separate browser workspace with its own cookies, allowing the demo to represent another user.
The visible indication of which control will respond to keyboard input.
Previously received information that may no longer match the current shared records.
The point when new features stop so the team can test, fix and rehearse.
Detailed development information that can expose internal settings if shown publicly.

decision.title: Describe reported activity honestly

options.name: Active check-in counts
options.good: Shows exactly what students have reported.
options.bad: Cannot establish whether a room is free.
options.fit: Works with the PDF and the team's limited build time.

options.name: Free/busy labels from check-ins
options.good: Very quick to understand.
options.bad: Zero reports can falsely suggest an occupied or booked room is free.
options.fit: The team lacks the evidence needed to support these labels.

decision.why: Missing reports are not evidence of an empty room. Honest counts still demonstrate shared student reporting and give Noor a credible explanation of the project's limits.
decision.disagreement: Replace the brief's promised free/busy status with reported activity. Do not claim verified availability.

decision.title: Use a list for the first release

options.name: Room list grouped by building
options.good: Easy to scan on phones and build from the PDF.
options.bad: Does not provide directions.
options.fit: Fits Tom's React skills and leaves time for shared check-ins and testing.

options.name: Campus map
options.good: Helps students understand locations.
options.bad: Needs reliable coordinates and additional interface work.
options.fit: Coordinates are not supplied; this adds uncertainty within 24 hours.

decision.why: The list satisfies the brief and uses the data already available. Put the map after the hackathon.

decision.title: Protect time for a reliable demonstration

options.name: Core flow with contingency
options.good: Leaves time for fixes, phone testing and pitch rehearsal.
options.bad: Has fewer visible features.
options.fit: Uses 36 of 52 person-hours and supports all three judging criteria.

options.name: Add a stretch feature before the pitch
options.good: Could add presentation appeal.
options.bad: Consumes the time needed to make the core demonstration dependable.
options.fit: Too risky with only 24 elapsed hours and three part-time allocations.

decision.why: Reserve 16 hours, or 30.8% of available effort. Freeze features six hours before the pitch and use any spare time to improve clarity and reliability.

decision.title: Application structure

options.name: React served by Flask
options.good: Uses both developers’ skills; one public address and deployment.
options.bad: Requires a small frontend build step.
options.fit: Fits Tom’s React experience and Ilias’s Flask experience.

options.name: Flask templates with plain JavaScript
options.good: Fewer build tools.
options.bad: Loses the benefit of Tom’s React experience.
options.fit: Possible, but offers little deadline benefit.

decision.why: Use one repository with small frontend and backend folders. Drop microservices, Kubernetes, separate frontend hosting, and additional database implementations.

decision.title: Hosting and persistent storage

options.name: Render with PostgreSQL; local PostgreSQL fallback
options.good: Public HTTPS phone access and one storage implementation.
options.bad: Hosting can sleep; local PostgreSQL needs setup.
options.fit: Primary choice, with deployment, learning, and fallback time explicitly budgeted.

options.name: Laptop-only Flask and PostgreSQL
options.good: Free offline demo using the same application and database code.
options.bad: Demonstrates two laptop browsers rather than shared campus phone access.
options.fit: Fallback if hosting cannot be proved within its allowance.

decision.picked: Render with PostgreSQL; local PostgreSQL fallback
decision.why: Use HTTPS for the two-phone milestone. Rehearse offline with two separate laptop browser profiles and localhost-only settings. Remove the proposed SQLite implementation. Hosted local files are temporary, so PostgreSQL remains the hosted store. [Storage limits](https://render.com/docs/free).

decision.title: Room presentation and status meaning

options.name: Building list with active check-ins
options.good: Works with the PDF and scans quickly on phones.
options.bad: Cannot guarantee available seats.
options.fit: Fits Noor’s design work without collecting coordinates.

options.name: Map with active check-ins
options.good: Helps locate unfamiliar buildings.
options.bad: Needs location data and extra interface work.
options.fit: Too much work for this deadline.

decision.why: Use “No active reports — availability unknown” and “3 active check-ins” consistently in responses, screens, and pitch examples. Neither zero nor positive counts establish free/full status.
decision.disagreement: The brief’s free/busy promise exceeds the available evidence. Use reported use and unknown availability in the pitch.

decision.title: Updating other phones

options.name: Poll every 15 seconds
options.good: Simple requests and failure handling.
options.bad: Other phones can lag by 15 seconds.
options.fit: Small implementation cost within 24 hours.

options.name: Persistent live connection
options.good: Pushes changes immediately.
options.bad: Adds connection recovery and server coordination.
options.fit: Little judging benefit compared with finishing and rehearsing.

decision.why: Refresh the acting phone immediately. Stop polling hidden tabs and slow retries after failures.

decision.title: Check-in identity

options.name: Random browser token
options.good: No login integration or student identity collection.
options.bad: One person can create reports through several browsers.
options.fit: Enough for a clearly labelled crowd-reporting prototype.

options.name: University account login
options.good: Could limit reports per account.
options.bad: Needs university integration details and potentially approval.
options.fit: Deferred beyond the hackathon.

decision.why: Allow one active check-in per token, verify ownership, and rate-limit writes. Combine explicit SameSite cookies with server origin checks. Counts represent active check-ins, not verified unique students.

decision.title: Handling forgotten checkout

options.name: Expire after 60 minutes with manual renewal
options.good: Bounds stale reports without background jobs or location tracking.
options.bad: Long sessions need renewal; forgotten exits remain temporarily.
options.fit: Small, testable prototype rule.

options.name: Keep check-ins until checkout
options.good: Simplest interaction.
options.bad: Abandoned reports accumulate.
options.fit: Undermines the entry’s usefulness.

decision.picked: Expire after 60 minutes with manual renewal
decision.why: Treat 60 minutes as a prototype setting, not a measured campus norm. Show expiry and renewal; an open page never renews presence.

decision.title: Identity for check-ins

options.name: Anonymous browser session
options.good: No passwords, email collection, or account setup.
options.bad: New browsers can create extra identities; presence cannot be verified.
options.fit: Fits the deadline and existing React/Flask skills.

options.name: University login
options.good: Could restrict participation to campus accounts.
options.bad: Needs university access and setup that are not provided; still cannot prove presence.
options.fit: Defer as the brief allows.

options.name: Email sign-in link
options.good: Avoids storing passwords.
options.bad: Adds email delivery, personal data, and link security work.
options.fit: Too much setup for this free, 24-hour entry.

decision.why: Keep the demo easy to join. Authorize writes using the server-issued session, never a user identifier supplied in the request. Accept and explain that anonymous participation cannot prevent all false reports.

decision.title: Public room status

options.name: Reported check-in totals
options.good: Useful signals without exposing individual identities.
options.bad: Counts are incomplete and may be false; small counts can reveal presence indirectly.
options.fit: Works with the PDF and voluntary check-ins.

options.name: Free/busy labels
options.good: Very quick to understand.
options.bad: Suggests verified availability despite missing occupancy and capacity data.
options.fit: Cannot support the promise made by the brief.

decision.why: Show “3 active check-ins” or “No active reports — availability unknown.” Explain that reports expire and do not reserve seats. The three-minute pitch should state this limitation.
decision.disagreement: The requested free/busy status is not supported by a room-name PDF and voluntary reports.

decision.title: Check-in lifetime

options.name: Expire after 60 minutes
options.good: Limits stale counts and makes stored entries eligible for cleanup.
options.bad: Students staying longer must renew; deletion waits for a request or manual cleanup.
options.fit: Small implementation with visible expiry text.

options.name: Keep until checkout
options.good: No renewal interruption.
options.bad: Forgotten checkouts persist and mislead others.
options.fit: Too unreliable for the main demo claim.

decision.why: Use server time and explicit renewal. Exclude expired entries from every count immediately. Delete expired records on the next request; sleeping hosting can delay deletion indefinitely. Ilias clears stored check-ins and sessions after the event.

decision.title: Finding a room

options.name: Building-grouped list
options.good: Fast to scan and easy to build from the PDF.
options.bad: Does not show walking routes.
options.fit: Uses the available room names and buildings without extra data or paid tools.

options.name: Campus map
options.good: Shows rooms in relation to the student's location.
options.bad: Needs reliable locations and more interface work.
options.fit: Too much uncertainty for the 24-hour deadline and 52 working hours.

decision.why: The list delivers the main task with the data already available. It leaves time for a reliable demo and readable phone screens.

decision.title: Describing room availability

options.name: Reported activity
options.good: Clearly separates student reports from verified availability.
options.bad: Cannot promise a free seat.
options.fit: Works with voluntary check-ins and the PDF.

options.name: Free or busy labels
options.good: Very quick to understand.
options.bad: Suggests certainty that the app cannot support.
options.fit: Unsuitable without booking, occupancy or capacity data.

decision.why: Show “3 active check-ins” or “No active check-ins — availability unknown.” Include when data was last updated. Avoid “full,” occupancy percentages and green “free” badges.
decision.disagreement: The brief asks for free/busy status, but check-ins cannot establish it. The pitch should describe finding rooms using recent student reports.

decision.title: Where check-in happens

options.name: Room detail and confirmation
options.good: Makes the selected room clear and keeps checkout easy to find.
options.bad: Adds one tap compared with checking in from the list.
options.fit: Three small screens can reuse the same room card and detail layout.

options.name: Check-in buttons on every list card
options.good: Offers the shortest possible action.
options.bad: Crowds phone screens and makes wrong-room taps easier.
options.fit: Saves a tap but adds avoidable confusion during the live demo.

decision.why: Tap a room, then tap “I’m here.” Show confirmation only after the server accepts it. Keep a “Your check-in” link visible for quick checkout. Include explicit renewal and expiry in this same layout.
